article_paragraphs: Imagining a collage of objects of American culture, the mind conjures up images of things like sports stadiums, a drive-thru menu, the Wall Street Bull, the Hollywood sign, blue jeans, apple pie, and likely, some kind of car. Cars, our car dependency, and the American love for V8 engines are integral to our culture, and there are no cars to demonstrate this better than the pony car family. While very similar, there are some differences between a muscle car and a pony car.

To put it simply, the muscle car and the pony car are two sides of the same coin. The muscle car was bigger and purely focused on looking cool and going fast, with not much thought to anything else. The pony car took all that was fun about the muscle car, including the good looks and exciting performance, and made it all a bit easier to live with, often by being smaller than its muscle car counterparts. The Mustang started the pony car trend, but it wasn't the only one to do it. Since those early days in the 1960s, we've seen different takes from different manufacturers, including models like the Chevrolet Camaro, the Dodge Challenger, and even some from the hands of Carroll Shelby. Many of these models have stuck around to the modern day. The spirit of the pony car is old, but it is far from gone.

The Chevrolet Camaro and the Ford Mustang have been in a constant battle for the pony car crown since the 1960s. As they chug on and on, new trims and upgrades grace each car, and in 1969, we saw a Camaro born of the pure rebellious nature a pony car should represent. The legend of the ZL1 starts with a man called Fred Gibb. Gibb was a Chevrolet dealer who was particularly sick of the brand's internal practices. The Corvette was the monarch of the Chevrolet lineup, and Chevy wanted to keep it that way. It adamantly ensured that no performance car other than the Corvette could be fitted with an engine with over 400 cubic inches of displacement. Gibb was sick of this favoritism, and he knew the Camaro could be so much more. So, he did something about it.

Gibb contacted Chevy's Central Office Production Order, a division charged with custom orders for mundane civil and municipal services, building things like taxi cabs or police cars. Ordering from COPO was something like a deli sandwich counter for cars with no questions asked. You could mix and match parts, and that's exactly what Gibb wanted. He ordered 50 Camaros stripped down for light weight and fitted with 430-horsepower, 427-cubic-inch V8s sourced from Chevy's Can-Am race cars. Chevrolet quickly wised up to Gibb's loophole and shut down production, but the original ZL1 remains the stuff of pony car legend.

The ZL1 is Chevy's story of childhood rebellion, and even though Chevy didn't see the greatness of a high-powered stripped-down Camaro originally, it eventually came around to the idea. To see just how far the company has come from its Corvette-rules-all philosophy, we can look at the most recent, and final, example of the ZL1 from 2024.

What would have been blasphemy in 1969 was now standard procedure, as the 2024 ZL1 was powered by a pushrod V8 pulled straight from the C7 generation Corvette making 650 horsepower thanks to some help from a supercharger. Keeping classic pony car character, the ZL1 sends all that power strictly to the rear wheels, and it can be distributed via either a 10-speed automatic or a six speed manual transmission. If you really want to turn things up, you can opt for the 1LE package, which throws in some extra upgrades, and you don't have to go through COPO to do it. The 1LE adds some stickier tires, carbon fiber everywhere, adjustable suspension, and a rear seat delete. It's Chevrolet's love letter to a car it originally didn't want to exist.

So, the Camaro has its defiant ZL1 package, but what does the Mustang have to match it? The answer is the Shelby GT500, whose original iteration came before the ZL1 in 1967. If you know a thing or two about Ford performance cars, you'll recognize the name Shelby. Before Carroll Shelby ever had a Mustang with his name on it, he was busy stuffing his nimble European-esque Cobras with massive Ford engines that had no business being there and helping Ford beat Ferrari at Le Mans. After that former achievement, in 1967, Shelby convinced Ford to put the Le Mans-based and Le Mans-winning 428 V8 into the Mustang. And so, the GT500 was born.

Prior to the GT500, Ford had already made the GT350, which was raucously fast but a bit unpolished. The GT500 took the GT350 recipe, smoothed out the edges, and eliminated the almost homemade character. By no means did this mean that the GT500 was a tame car, though. Covered in aggressive aerodynamic body panels of fiberglass for lighter weight, the GT500's V8 made 355 horsepower, and could cover the quarter mile in 15 seconds, ripping past the line at 95 mph. It was a race-bred Mustang for the road, a hot-rodder's garage build in a suit and a Stetson, and it was one of the wickedly cool cars that made Carroll Shelby a legend.

title: Leclerc loses two points for repeating his 'GP2 move
raw_summary: Charles Leclerc has been penalised for his overtake on Liam Lawson in Formula 1’s Brazilian Grand Prix, with the stewards reversing the result of that pass. Leclerc spent a lot of the race outside the top 10, having started down in 14th, but he enjoyed a more competitive final stint on the intermediates, which included passing Lawson on the penultimate lap.

Leclerc spent a lot of the race outside the top 10, having started down in 14th, but he enjoyed a more competitive final stint on the intermediates, which included passing Lawson on the penultimate lap.
article_paragraphs: Charles Leclerc has been penalised for his overtake on Liam Lawson in Formula 1’s Brazilian Grand Prix, with the stewards reversing the result of that pass.

Leclerc spent a lot of the race outside the top 10, having started down in 14th, but he enjoyed a more competitive final stint on the intermediates, which included passing Lawson on the penultimate lap.
That move started with Leclerc making contact with Lawson at the end of the previous lap, at the apex of the Turn 12 Juncao corner.
The duo continued to fight until Leclerc got ahead exiting the Senna S and pulled clear, crossing the line in seventh place.
But both drivers had to see the stewards after the race, with Leclerc penalised.

“While the contact was minor and Lawson was able to maintain the [position] thereafter, Lawson claimed that the contact damaged the rear left rim of his car, and also enabled Leclerc to get closer to him on track and then eventually overtake him five corners later," the stewards' verdict read.
“Furthermore, under the driving standard guidelines, Lawson had the right to the corner and it was for Leclerc to take the necessary steps to avoid a collision.
“Leclerc that it was a minor contact with no obvious sporting consequence.

raw_summary: When we consider whether we can afford a car, so much of the focus tends to be on the sticker price that we often forget that the costs don't stop once we've made our purchase. Small, everyday expenses that come alongside, like fuel, servicing, finance interest, depreciation, insurance, and tax, aren't always obvious, but the true cost of car ownership adds up over time . With that in mind, the car valuation experts at AAA performed a study to investigate car ownership costs in 2026. It turns out that drivers are facing ongoing price increases, with the AAA 2026 Your Driving Costs study revealing that the annual cost of owning and running a new car has soared to $12,863, or $1,071.92 per month this year. That's up from an average of $11,577 or $964.78 per month in 2025.

Small, everyday expenses that come alongside, like fuel, servicing, finance interest, depreciation, insurance, and tax, aren't always obvious, but the true cost of car ownership adds up over time .

With that in mind, the car valuation experts at AAA performed a study to investigate car ownership costs in 2026. It turns out that drivers are facing ongoing price increases, with the AAA 2026 Your Driving Costs study revealing that the annual cost of owning and running a new car has soared to $12,863, or $1,071.92 per month this year. That's up from an average of $11,577 or $964.78 per month in 2025.

At that rate, ownership costs can add 32.67% on top of the $39,376 sales-weighted average MSRP of new vehicles. The larger bills have been linked to surging fuel prices, faster depreciation, and higher finance interest rates. Still, your specific costs can vary greatly, depending on your car's fuel type.

Owning any car at all is getting more expensive , but the AAA study revealed something more fundamental: Electric cars cost more to own than their traditional fuel-powered and hybrid counterparts. That's largely because depreciation on EVs is worse than gas or hybrid cars. On top of that, those who drive electric cars face higher fees and finance costs. Where EVs tend to do better is in fuel expenses, as they typically cost 66% to 70% less to run than gasoline cars.

Looking at a set of average consumption figures, AAA found that regular-grade gasoline costs $4.152 per gallon on average, while electric cars charged at home averaged as little as 18 cents per kilowatt hour. EVs have seen smaller electricity rate increases, too. The AAA data shows electricity prices have jumped 7.8% since 2025, while gas costs have increased a shocking 31.8%.

Even so, owning and running EVs costs more than gas-powered models, due to higher fees, finance costs, and depreciation, with certain EVs said to depreciate about twice as fast as their gas-powered counterparts. That contributed to pushing EV ownership costs above gas-powered models across the medium sedan, compact SUV, and pickup truck segments.

Nowhere is that gap more pronounced than in the medium sedan segment, where gas-powered medium sedans cost $3,080 less to own (at $10,582 per year) than comparable EV medium sedans ($13,662). Hybrids are even cheaper (at $10,204) and cost the least to own in every category, including the medium SUV class, where EVs win back some ground against gas-powered models, costing $14,332 versus $14,431 for gasoline SUVs.

As a car owner, every mile you drive costs money, but it is entirely possible to keep costs down. One way to do this is to shop around for cheaper insurance. Compare quotes from providers, or even consider buying a car from one of the cheapest brands to insure .

raw_title: Tesla Cybertruck Tires Aren't Cheap To Replace: Here's What They Cost
title: Tesla Cybertruck Tires Aren't Cheap To Replace: Here's What They Cost
raw_summary: The Tesla Cybertruck is one of the most polarizing vehicles of our time, largely due to its unconventional silhouette and the lack of curves on its stainless steel body. Besides grabbing the attention of onlookers, owners have another thing to worry about that has to do with maintenance costs — the tires. Changing the rubber on your Tesla pickup truck requires a higher budget than your average full-size truck, and can exceed the $2,000 mark on flagship trims. Furthermore, the Cybertruck's tires might need to be replaced sooner than expected due to its immense weight and torque figures. Of course this is not limited to Tesla, as the Rivian R1T suffers from similar issues. According to Tesla's manual, the entry-level Cybertruck with 18-inch wheels wears all-season Goodyear Wrangler Territory HT rubber (285/70R18). Stepping up to 20-inch wheels, you can either have all-season Pirelli Scorpion ATR tires (285/65R20), or the heavier-duty Goodyear Wrangler Territory R/T (LT285/65R20). The latter feature a bespoke sidewall design tailored for the wheel covers of the Cybertruck . Finally, owners in cold regions can opt for the 20-inch Goodyear Wrangler DuraTrac R/T.

article_paragraphs: The Tesla Cybertruck is one of the most polarizing vehicles of our time, largely due to its unconventional silhouette and the lack of curves on its stainless steel body. Besides grabbing the attention of onlookers, owners have another thing to worry about that has to do with maintenance costs — the tires. Changing the rubber on your Tesla pickup truck requires a higher budget than your average full-size truck, and can exceed the $2,000 mark on flagship trims. Furthermore, the Cybertruck's tires might need to be replaced sooner than expected due to its immense weight and torque figures.

Of course this is not limited to Tesla, as the Rivian R1T suffers from similar issues. According to Tesla's manual, the entry-level Cybertruck with 18-inch wheels wears all-season Goodyear Wrangler Territory HT rubber (285/70R18). Stepping up to 20-inch wheels, you can either have all-season Pirelli Scorpion ATR tires (285/65R20), or the heavier-duty Goodyear Wrangler Territory R/T (LT285/65R20). The latter feature a bespoke sidewall design tailored for the wheel covers of the Cybertruck . Finally, owners in cold regions can opt for the 20-inch Goodyear Wrangler DuraTrac R/T.

The cheapest 18-inch Cybertruck option costs $1,474 per set from independent retailers, while the heavy-duty 20-inch tires with the unique design will set you back $2,120 if you buy it directly from Tesla. An OEM 20-inch Core Wheel and Pirelli Winter Tire Package is priced at $3,650, but you'll need an extra $320for the wheel covers.

Cybertruck owners looking outside factory options have access to a greater variety. Searching at Tire Rack for Cybertruck-compatible rubber, we found prices starting from $996 for an Advanta ATX 20-inch set and climbing to $2,149 for a set of Goodyear Wrangler Territory R/T 20-inch tires. Tesla tuner Unplugged Performance offers tire sets starting at $1,728 for the 18-inch BFGoodrich All-Terrain T/A KO3 and climbing to $3,164 for 24-inch Nitto Recon Grappler rubber (295/45R24). The same company also sells complete wheel-and-tire packages ranging from $3,957 to $11,195 per set of four.

While we covered the prices of Tesla Cybertruck tires, it's worth noting how they compare with the rest of the full-size truck competition. Starting with ICE-powered models, tire changes can be significantly cheaper. A 17-inch Yokohama Geolandar M/T G003 set for the updated 2027 Ford F-150 starts at $480, while the 18-inch Bridgestone Dueler H/P Sport costs $574 per set. Similarly, 18-inch options for the Chevy Silverado start at $621, for the Ram 1500 at $688, and for the Toyota Tundra at $492.

If you stick to 18-inch wheels, one of the most expensive options for the aforementioned trucks is the Toyo Tires Open Country M/T (LT275/70R18) priced at $1,715 per set. The electric Rivian R1T is closer to Tesla territory with a cost of $2,216 per set of 22-inch Nokian Hakkapeliitta R5 SUV winter tires or up to $5,981 for one of the available wheel-and-tire sets on the official website. In any case, the cost of tire changes is something you need to consider before ordering the largest model in the Tesla lineup, or a similarly-sized electric truck.

title: Fallout & Drama: Who Won And Who Lost At F1's 2026 Brazilian Grand Prix
raw_summary: Mercedes clinching the 2026 Formula 1 constructors’ championship with its first podium-less race of the season summed this wild Brazilian Grand Prix, as an extremely mixed up grid and constantly changing weather teamed up to create plenty of entertainment. Lando Norris rated this as one of his best wins, and it’s hard to argue, because there were plenty of chances to get it wrong.

article_paragraphs: Mercedes clinching the 2026 Formula 1 constructors’ championship with its first podium-less race of the season summed this wild Brazilian Grand Prix, as an extremely mixed up grid and constantly changing weather teamed up to create plenty of entertainment.
Lando Norris rated this as one of his best wins, and it’s hard to argue, because there were plenty of chances to get it wrong.

He lost the lead on the run to Turn 1 and was then muscled out of second by Liam Lawson into Turn 2. By the time the poleman got Lawson back into the Bico de Pato on lap six, he was over five seconds behind Kimi Antonelli and a win was doable but difficult.

His race turned on the first big call. McLaren brought Norris in for slicks a lap before Mercedes did the same with Antonelli, and that extra lap on warm tyres let Norris slash the gap and pounce once Antonelli started to slip up.
After that, he made no mistakes in conditions where Antonelli, among others, made plenty. - Scott Mitchell-Malm
Is it churlish to put the Mercedes pair in the Losers column on the day when Mercedes finally ended a constructors’ title drought dating back to 2021?

Maybe. But Mercedes only clinched the constructors’ title today. It effectively won that months ago. And if Ferrari hadn’t had such an abject disaster of a race, Mercedes’ party might’ve had to wait until Las Vegas.

Because the Brazilian GP itself was just sketchy for Mercedes and its new drivers’ champion - Kimi Antonelli spinning away the race lead and slithering down the field to fifth with a so-far undiagnosed problem that team boss Toto Wolff thinks was probably just a set-up or tyre pressure miscue with big consequences. An unsafe pit release penalty didn't cost him a position, but somewhat typified his day.

title: F1 2026's best race? Our verdict on Brazil chaos
raw_summary: Formula 1 2026's best race? A preview for F1 2027? A template for reverse grid races or a cautionary warning against them? A chaotic Brazilian Grand Prix gave us plenty to think about. There's always a terrible risk that the run-in ends up being really flat and low energy, with a collection of dead-rubber races, once the main championship is decided early.

article_paragraphs: Formula 1 2026's best race? A preview for F1 2027? A template for reverse grid races or a cautionary warning against them? A chaotic Brazilian Grand Prix gave us plenty to think about.
There's always a terrible risk that the run-in ends up being really flat and low energy, with a collection of dead-rubber races, once the main championship is decided early.

That's especially the case when the runaway champion is still a decent contender to win the remaining races. Fortunately, we have a good stab at seeing strong race-by-race narratives even without a (drivers') title on the line. And you can always count on Interlagos to throw up something special in a season!
What was there not to enjoy about today? I can't remember a race that had so much packed into it.

A change of lead at the start, Liam Lawson briefly running second, Lewis Hamilton's absurd opening lap, Max Verstappen's much more sustained and spectacular charge to second, George Russell spinning in the pitlane (that's rare!), Kimi Antonelli chucking it off while leading (then again to lose out on a podium, almost as rare!)...

The only thing it was missing was a close fight for victory. But even that disappointment is tempered by the knowledge that Norris produced a really classy drive that I hope a lot of people can appreciate the quality of.
I'll be counting down the laps if/when F1 races in Abu Dhabi, for I have immensely low hopes for that race, and even Qatar, regardless of any wider debate over those races.
So if the season nosedives into an anti-climax, we'll always have Brazil...

title: Watch The 2027 Hyundai Tucson Get Hurled Around The Nürburgring Like A Huge Miata
raw_summary: There's nothing quite like watching a vehicle get driven in ways you never expected. Think Miatas on a rally stage in Finland or a bunch of smoky pickup trucks on a race track in Thailand . There's something gratifying about seeing things taken to new extremes, and we probably all have a story or two about ripping a beater or rental car in ways that most wouldn't. But if you're a test driver, it's your duty to drive cars, trucks, and SUVs in ways most wouldn't. And if you're working for Hyundai, that means hurling a 2027 Tucson, before it goes on sale, around the Nürburgring Nordschleife — seemingly the world's most famous test track — like a huge Miata. Sure, Porsche, BMW, Audi, and Mercedes-Benz test drivers probably have a great time wringin' out their steeds on this German track's sacred surface, but we bet the Hyundai cats are having just as much (or possibly more) fun.

Think Miatas on a rally stage in Finland or a bunch of smoky pickup trucks on a race track in Thailand . There's something gratifying about seeing things taken to new extremes, and we probably all have a story or two about ripping a beater or rental car in ways that most wouldn't.

But if you're a test driver, it's your duty to drive cars, trucks, and SUVs in ways most wouldn't. And if you're working for Hyundai, that means hurling a 2027 Tucson, before it goes on sale, around the Nürburgring Nordschleife — seemingly the world's most famous test track — like a huge Miata. Sure, Porsche, BMW, Audi, and Mercedes-Benz test drivers probably have a great time wringin' out their steeds on this German track's sacred surface, but we bet the Hyundai cats are having just as much (or possibly more) fun.

It isn't all a big joke, though, because manufacturers have to explore a vehicle's limits to truly poke and prod it for deficiencies. But it looks freaking epic. Man, what we'd give to sit shotgun on this stilted-up rollercoaster ride.

What makes testing cars at the Nürburgring so special? Well, for one, claiming a fastest production car record. There's a good chance that this isn't the case with the flyin' 2027 Hyundai Tucson , but hey, it's probably a good idea to keep an idea on the company's upcoming news coverage just in case.

However, more realistic: there's the fact that it's a very long (almost 13 miles) and variety-rich track with big undulations, flowing sweepers, big elevation changes, on- and off-camber bits, high-speed sections, jumps, as well as the ability to be bone-dry on one end and raining on the other. Germany's Eiffel, where the 'Ring is located, is a climate that's rich in rain that comes and goes in the blink of an eye. Testing the Tucson's suspension, brakes, and their relationship with the tires' grip here gives engineers a good idea where the limits are in a bunch of scenarios. Additionally, the high speed gives them an idea of how well the cooling system works, how well the brakes work, as well as if the engine and transmission will have any issues. If it can survive a flying lap here, it's definitely good for service in normal, everyday driving.

Plus, it helps that Hyundai maintains a facility right nearby. The brand tunes all of its high-performance N models on the 'Ring, which undergo stricter and more extensive testing than non-performance fare. The plain ol' Tucson may not get that same exact treatment (yet), but it's cool to see them still driving 'em on there like they stole 'em

title: So You've Hit A Deer With Your Car. Now What?

Typical fall, right? That last one ain't no joke — just about everyone who has driven in a place with a significant deer population can tell you a tale or two about a run-in with deer. article_paragraphs: Fall is a magical time of year: The air is alive with the scent of pumpkin spice, the decorative gourds are presented, and, of course, the dang deer won't stay off the roads. Typical fall, right? That last one ain't no joke — just about everyone who has driven in a place with a significant deer population can tell you a tale or two about a run-in with deer. If you're in France, you really need to look out for the drunk deer.

Deer are a hazard drivers have to contend with. Sure, we could put some murder kitties in the forests, because more big cats in forests can reduce car crashes by roughly 75% . Or, we could install crossings to give creatures a safe path over big roads, like they did in California with the world's largest wildlife crossing . But short of that, accidents with deer will happen. State Farm reports that there were more than 1.6 million animal-related collisions between July 2025 and July 2026. It is a real concern.

But don't fret. If the unfortunate accident does happen, the first thing you should do is to ensure your own safety. Move off the road, and turn on your hazard lights so you're not at risk from any other vehicles. Check your vehicle only when it's safe to do so. There's no need to compound the accident by putting yourself in greater danger.

Hopefully, you are in a safer situation now, so be sure to check any passengers and yourself for injuries. Call 911 immediately if anyone is injured. At this point, you may be tempted to check on the deer. If you can see it and it's a road hazard, for safety's sake, report it. You don't want another driver to hit it. Do not attempt to approach or move it! An injured animal is a dangerous animal. If it's not visible, don't try to find it.

At this point, it's not a bad idea to take pictures of the accident in case your insurance asks for it. Your insurance may also ask for an accident report, so it's a good idea to get one. Speaking of insurance, hitting a deer is usually covered under comprehensive coverage if you have it. Swerving to miss a deer and hitting something else is typically covered by collision coverage, but don't do that.

If your vehicle is not drivable, call a tow truck. If you think your car is still drivable, you may be tempted to leave. If there is property damage or if the deer is still a hazard to others, report it. Otherwise, depending on state law, you may be okay to leave. Before you drive off, do a basic check of your vehicle to ensure that it's actually roadworthy. Take a look underneath your vehicle to see if it is leaking any fluids. If it is, do not drive it — you can cause more damage to your engine. Check that the hood is latched securely and will not come loose. Verify the headlights are still working, especially when it's dark out. Simple stuff, but it could save you trouble down the road.

There is no sure-fire way to avoid hitting a deer, but you can reduce your risk by being cautious when you're in an area with an active deer population. Slow down to a speed that will allow you a better chance of stopping before they become hood ornaments. Be especially cautious at dawn and dusk, as deer are more prone to roam at those times of day. Use extra caution when traveling near wildlife crossing signs. No, the deer aren't reading those signs and deciding to cross there – obviously, those signs declare that you are in an area known to have heavy activity. Also, remember that deer tend to travel in groups, so if you see one, others are likely nearby.

Lastly, if hitting that deer is unavoidable, your natural instinct will be to swerve to avoid the animal. Fight the urge to do this. Swerving to miss the deer is often more dangerous, as it can cause your car to roll or result in other unwanted behavior. Quite often, the resulting crash is worse than just hitting the deer. Brake in a straight line, and brace for impact.

As part of Dr Andrew Forrest’s vision of real zero by 2030, Fortescue is installing wind turbines with a blade length of 89 metres. Bigger than Godzilla! Have we got your attention now? The blades will be deployed at the Nullagine Wind Farm in the Pilbara region of Western Australia. They will arrive by ship at the Port Headland project site. Fortescue has done major upgrades to allow the blades easy access and to minimise impact on local traffic. The community will also receive regular updates throughout the delivery program to keep residents informed.

For global readers, I would like to point out that Fortescue’s mining operations and land tenements in the Pilbara region of Western Australia cover more than 87,000 square kilometres (34,000 square miles). This is roughly the size of Austria (83,879 km²), Ireland (84,421 km²), or Serbia (88,361 km²), and more than twice the size of countries like the Netherlands (41,850 km²) or Switzerland (41,285 km²). And for USA readers, Fortescue’s land holdings alone are larger than South Carolina, West Virginia, or Maryland, and roughly the same size as the entire state of Maine or Indiana. But only one eighth the size of Texas.

You will have read about Twiggy Forrest’s achievements and vision of real zero mining operations here and here . Fortescue is taking steps to educate the public on decarbonisation. You need to take the people with you, especially the shareholders. Here is a great video produced by Fortescue to show how to decode decarbonisation . The Godzilla-sized wind turbines are part of an ecosystem. They will provide the power to recharge the electric dump trucks. But just how do you recharge a 240 ton dump truck in a timely manner? Using 6MW robotic fast charging, of course, thus eliminating 26% of Fortescue’s emissions — and saving a dump truck of money in the process.

CleanTechnica reported on the acquisition of Williams Racing 5 years ago, in order for Fortescue to access Williams’ fast-charging technology. It has taken some time, but it looks like everything is coming together. I still have the picture in my head, inspired by this acquisition, of huge dump trucks doing F1 races in the red dust of the Australian Outback. Beyond the fantasies of Mad Max, even. While we are indulging in mental gymnastics, the Fortescue video tells us that 6MW of charging is like boiling 1,875 electric kettles all at once. That’s a lot of tea or coffee! A less than 30-minute charge will give 4 hours of operation for the truck. The charging equipment has to be resilient, as the Pilbara is hot and dusty, with temperatures in summer over 40 degrees and down to below freezing on winter nights.

Episode 2 answers the question “Can a green grid power a mining operation 24/7?” It’s a big ask. Fortescue is the fourth largest iron ore producer in the world, exporting 200 million tons a year. The advantages: Fortescue achieves cost savings, does good for the climate, and keeps control of its energy. In the current global situation, I would add energy security.

The Pilbara has 300 days a year of irradiation and Fortescue plans to harvest that with a planned 1.5 gigawatts of solar farms. Eventually, this will be backed up with 900 MW wind and balanced by 5 GWh of battery storage — enough electricity to power 800,000 homes on solar alone. This is all connected by a high-voltage green grid consisting of 600 km of transmission lines. “A city scale power system in the middle of nowhere.” The green operation does not draw from the public grid; not the distant future, but right now.

title: AI Comes For Drag Racers' Jobs As GM Patents Automated Launch Control
raw_summary: AI is coming for all of us. Not necessarily in an apocalyptic world like "The Terminator" or "The Matrix," but by stealing jobs from truck drivers , astronauts , and even Jalopnik writers (despite what I read in the comments, I assure you we're all human beings — at least, for now). Not even drag racers are safe, thanks to a launch control system GM patented that not only automates the launch process, but even reads the countdown Christmas tree to time a perfect launch. Patents can be wordy and cumbersome to read, but Road & Track sums this one up nicely. Some cars already have launch control systems, which can get you off the line as quickly as possible with the perfect balance of power and traction. Pair those systems with the cameras being used in cars today and the rest is a simple matter of programming.

article_paragraphs: AI is coming for all of us. Not necessarily in an apocalyptic world like "The Terminator" or "The Matrix," but by stealing jobs from truck drivers , astronauts , and even Jalopnik writers (despite what I read in the comments, I assure you we're all human beings — at least, for now). Not even drag racers are safe, thanks to a launch control system GM patented that not only automates the launch process, but even reads the countdown Christmas tree to time a perfect launch.

Patents can be wordy and cumbersome to read, but Road & Track sums this one up nicely. Some cars already have launch control systems, which can get you off the line as quickly as possible with the perfect balance of power and traction. Pair those systems with the cameras being used in cars today and the rest is a simple matter of programming.

The potential future tech uses the car's cameras to recognize the Christmas tree lights at a drag strip, and a prompt instructs the driver to activate launch control. This part works like normal, with the driver pressing the gas and brake pedals simultaneously. Once launch control is engaged, the driver removes their feet from the pedals, and the car takes over. It doesn't just use its onboard cameras to watch the lights and go on green, it initiates the launch process before the light is green, ensuring the car begins to move precisely when it's supposed to without red-lighting or launching too early. This is exactly the way I learned to do it, but a computer is going to be far more precise than my feet. I'm only human.

Automatic drag strip launch control is a fine technological achievement. It also completely misses the point of what racing is all about: human drivers testing their skill against one another. Drag racing doesn't have the braking or handling challenges of a road course or rally stage , but it still requires skill to reduce your reaction time and execute even a near-perfect launch. If you take that out of the equation by automating the entire process, what's left? Not steering into the wall? In a production car, that takes even less skill than driving down the highway. ( Top Fuel dragsters and Funny Cars are a completely different story. Mad respect to them.)

Does anyone really want autonomous racing ? I sure don't. In theory, a machine can always put down the perfect lap, time after time. The only time it gets exciting is when the programming goes wrong, and it steers straight into a wall . People already complain that Formula 1 is boring . It takes extraordinary driver talent to race at those speeds, but the cars are so good, so reliable, and so evenly matched that there's little difference between them. Take the driver out of the car, and it's nothing but a competition of technology. If I want to see that, I'd rather watch BattleBots . It's much more fun, and you get to watch them completely destroy each other.

I have never driven a perfect lap, and I never will. Perfection itself doesn't matter. It's the pursuit of perfection that matters. Striving to do better than we ever have before is rewarding for its own sake. It's also part of what makes us human. So I'll leave GM's drag strip launch control turned off and drop the clutch myself. I don't care that I'll run a slower time than the fully automated machine. As a certain James Bond villain once said , "There's no point in living if you can't feel alive."

Norris soon wrestled second back from Lawson, but Antonelli escaped down the road in the lead as the field waited for the right moment to switch from intermediate to slick tyres.
McLaren and Norris got that call right as he pitted a lap before Antonelli and closed a lot of that gap.
Antonelli struggled to fire up his soft tyres and ended up spinning at Turn 1 on his second lap, allowing Norris into the race lead.
Antonelli’s slide continued as the Red Bulls, Isack Hadjar and Max Verstappen, picked him off.
He reported his car was steering by itself, and he was struggling to get around the left-hand corners in particular.
Norris went unthreatened thereafter, building such a solid gap out front that even a late-rain shower and switch back to intermediates didn’t do anything to unsettle his grip on the lead.

Once again, BEVs (+8% YoY) and PHEVs (-9% YoY) are experiencing opposite dynamics. Pure electrics actually set a record high of 1.54 million registrations.
This means that, while plugin vehicle YTD growth remains low (+4% YoY), that is solely due to the PHEV blues (-10% YoY). BEVs are on their way back to normal (+12%).

Share-wise, September saw BEVs end the month at 23% share, with the plugin tally increasing to 32% if we add in PHEVs. This near-record performance pulled the 2026 plugin share to higher levels. BEVs are now at 18% , while plugin hybrids are at 7% . Therefore, 2026 EV share is now at 25% .

Looking at the best selling models , there’s some news. The leader Tesla Model Y hit a new all-time record (165,000 units), thanks to a 17% YoY growth rate. That larger six-seat version is doing wonders here.

The runner-up spot went to the Tesla Model 3. Despite being down 4% YoY, it picked up enough deliveries (65,000) to surpass both the small Geely Xingyuan, also known as the E2 or EX2 in export markets, and the BYD Song.
Regarding Geely’s hatchback, the export highlights were Brazil (2,724 units), Australia (1,211), Indonesia (1,890), and Thailand (1,759).

Despite being relegated to 4th, the BYD Song was actually the fastest grower among the top 5, rising 19% YoY and reaching 54,519 registrations. This was due to an export push (the highlights being Brazil — 5,892 units, Italy — 2,134 units, and Germany — 2,028 units) and the new-generation Ultra body. Flash charging capabilities promise to recharge the Song’s sales and make it a serious candidate, not only for the silver medal in 2026, but also as strong competition to the Tesla Model Y in off-peak months.

In a near-record month, records were plenty, with six models in the top 20 reaching record highs. Besides the aforementioned Tesla Model Y, all the other five record scorers were compact models — a coincidence or an indication of where the market is going?

summary: Pontiac had helped launch the muscle-car era in 1963 — when it debuted the GTO package for its 1964 Pontiac Tempest LeMans coupe — and the brand followed that up with the Firebird pony car in 1967. In 1969, both saw iconic variants take the stage.
article_paragraphs: Pontiac had helped launch the muscle-car era in 1963 — when it debuted the GTO package for its 1964 Pontiac Tempest LeMans coupe — and the brand followed that up with the Firebird pony car in 1967. In 1969, both saw iconic variants take the stage. The former began courting customers with a new GTO trim called The Judge , while the latter hatched the Firebird Trans Am.

Only, it wasn't called the Trans Am at first. The brand had originally tried out a variety of different ideas on the public, with "Sebring" coming out on top –- inspired, no doubt, by the country's oldest road-racing circuit, Sebring International Raceway in Sebring, Florida. Yet, when Pontiac went to register the name, it discovered Chrysler had gotten there first.

The public's next-most-popular names were "Formula" and "Trans Am," so Pontiac snapped up both. Trans Am was reserved for the most powerful member of the Firebird family, which was actually a little odd. General Motors was already running Camaros in the Sports Car Club of America's Trans Am series. Moreover, Pontiac's decision ran into a roadblock anyways. It turns out that the brand didn't have permission from the SCCA to use that moniker, at least not at first. Once the lawyers got involved, Pontiac agreed to pay the organization $5 for every Firebird Trans Am it produced.

Now, finding the exact amount forked over isn't easy, but in 1979 alone, for instance, enthusiast sites say that Pontiac made more than 117,000 Tran Ams. Royalties-wise, that works out to a non-negligible total of $585,000, which is equivalent to about $2.7 million today. Some sources say that — during some seasons — the Pontiac royalty check was all that kept the SCCA out of bankruptcy.

One of the reasons Pontiac didn't put up a fuss about the royalty deal was that it didn't think it would actually sell that many. The SCCA apparently didn't realize what was going on until 1970 or 1971, and the brand had only produced 697 Trans Ams during the model's first partial year on the market — it went on sale in April of 1969. For some context, the entire Firebird lineup, in what was considered a down year, was worth 87,709 sales during 1969.

But one of the main reasons the Trans Am was introduced was to boost demand for the Firebird family. Helping to attract enthusiast customers was a pretty comprehensive package of upgrades that would set you back $724.60 (for a total Trans Am base price that opened at about $3,600). The highlight was under the hood, where Pontiac placed a standard 400-cubic-inch V8 with a Ram Air III intake system good for 330 bhp. As an alternative, buyers could opt for a more powerful setup with 345 bhp. It's backed by the same displacement, plus high-lift cams and upgraded valves/pistons. Additionally, there were standard dynamic details such as front/rear spoilers, functional hood scoops, a ride-and-handling package, high-effort variable-ratio power steering, high-effort power front disc brakes, and dual exhaust. Of course, when it comes to exhaust outlets, two isn't always better than one .

All '69 Trans Ams were then wrapped in a Cameo White exterior accented by Tyrol Blue racing stripes. One thing that did set some apart, however, was the body style. The majority of the first-year cars – 689 -– were hardtops, but 8 were convertibles.

Currently presented by Pirelli — and originally known as the Trans American Sedan Championship — the series was just about to wrap up its 60th-anniversary season at the Circuit of the Americas when this article was written. The very first race was held in 1966, and in an interesting coincidence, it was at Sebring.

In 1969, both saw iconic variants take the stage.

title: Hungarian VW Bus Goes from 'Matchbox: The Movie' to Matchbox, the Toy Car
raw_summary: Filmed in Budapest and Bratislava, Matchbox: The Movie has a fairly tenuous connection to the little die-cast toys. Starring the always charismatic John Cena as a CIA agent racing to deal with a rogue nuclear weapon, the central conceit is that a group of friends who used to play together with Matchbox cars in middle school reunite in adulthood to take down the bad guys. It’s a movie that plays like a kid narrating a story while pushing die-cast cars around the carpet, which feels like a pretty good fit for the brand association. Compared to Hot Wheels, which are all about speed and pulling off loops on those iconic orange tracks, Matchbox as a brand skews a little more realistic, and often features construction machines and vintage vehicles.

Starring the always charismatic John Cena as a CIA agent racing to deal with a rogue nuclear weapon, the central conceit is that a group of friends who used to play together with Matchbox cars in middle school reunite in adulthood to take down the bad guys.
article_paragraphs: Filmed in Budapest and Bratislava, Matchbox: The Movie has a fairly tenuous connection to the little die-cast toys. Starring the always charismatic John Cena as a CIA agent racing to deal with a rogue nuclear weapon, the central conceit is that a group of friends who used to play together with Matchbox cars in middle school reunite in adulthood to take down the bad guys.

It’s a movie that plays like a kid narrating a story while pushing die-cast cars around the carpet, which feels like a pretty good fit for the brand association. Compared to Hot Wheels, which are all about speed and pulling off loops on those iconic orange tracks, Matchbox as a brand skews a little more realistic, and often features construction machines and vintage vehicles.

Speaking of iconic orange, one of the central vehicles onscreen is a 1970s Volkswagen T2, the beloved Microbus. These things are such a huge part of popular culture that one was the main plot point in an episode of Futurama , which saw the crew hopping into a VW Bus and following Beck’s band around. (Best joke: When asked by Professor Farnsworth where the onboard time dilation device is, Fry reaches under the seat and produces a bong.)

In this case, two VW T2s were used in filming, both owned by Budapest-based Dávid Sipos. One of the two needed sufficient modification for stunt driving that it ended up no longer road legal, but the more original of the pair survived the filming schedule unscathed and came back into Sipos’s possession. As a tie-in with the film, Mattel of course produced Matchbox models of the film cars, and Sipos was delighted to find that the blister-pack model of the VW Bus was a faithful match for his car, right down to the aftermarket sunroof and identical Hungarian license plate.

The story gets even better, with the involvement of the original owner who picked up the keys to this orange bus some 50 years ago. If a VW Microbus is a symbol of counterculture in the U.S., that’s not the case overseas. In 1964, reacting to European tariffs on U.S. chicken products, President Lyndon B. Johnson enacted the so-called “chicken tax,” slapping a 25 percent penalty on various products including imported European light trucks.

For Volkswagen, this meant the death knell of U.S.-exported T2 pickups and panel vans, so the Microbus was typically a passenger van stateside. In Europe, working T2s continued chugging along as part of the furniture of a busy city, getting people and goods where they needed to go.

This particular 1976 T2B was delivered by train to Budapest for the Hungarian Water Works to use as a service vehicle. A young employee with the last name Thaly drove it right off the rail car at the depot, and it entered fleet service for the next eight years.

By 1984, something more modern was needed, so the company offered the VW to Thaly, who promptly snapped it up. He kept working, but the T2 effectively enjoyed a sunny retirement, stored carefully in a garage and used as a summertime camping vehicle driven throughout Europe, first with his children, then with his grandchildren. This went on for three decades.

raw_title: Here's Why Fuel Economy Drops So Much At 75 MPH
title: Here's Why Fuel Economy Drops So Much At 75 MPH
raw_summary: It is a well known fact that combustion vehicles have greater fuel economy ratings on the highway rather than in urban driving scenarios. However, this reality can be easily reversed if you exceed a certain speed threshold. Setting the cruise control to 75 mph may seem to be a good compromise between travel time, safety, and fuel consumption. However, data proves you could be saving more money by easing off the throttle. Generally speaking, engines burn more fuel when they get pushed. But it's not only acceleration that forces an engine to work hard. Weight and aerodynamic resistance perform an important role in efficiency. So where does speed come into play? The math comes down to fluid dynamics. Aerodynamic drag force is directly proportional to air density, the object's frontal area, its streamlined shape, and the square of its speed. The "square" part is what makes speed more important than the other factors.

However, this reality can be easily reversed if you exceed a certain speed threshold. Setting the cruise control to 75 mph may seem to be a good compromise between travel time, safety, and fuel consumption. However, data proves you could be saving more money by easing off the throttle.

Generally speaking, engines burn more fuel when they get pushed. But it's not only acceleration that forces an engine to work hard. Weight and aerodynamic resistance perform an important role in efficiency. So where does speed come into play? The math comes down to fluid dynamics. Aerodynamic drag force is directly proportional to air density, the object's frontal area, its streamlined shape, and the square of its speed. The "square" part is what makes speed more important than the other factors.

According to government data from the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the fuel efficiency of a conventional midsize sedan travelling at 55 mph is 45 mpg. This figure drops to 38 mpg if you accelerate to 65 mph and takes a further dip to 32 mpg at 75 mph. The effect of these numbers is even more profound at a time when fuel prices have skyrocketed . Based on the current U.S. average price of $4.25 per gallon of regular gas, someone who covers 15,000 highway miles per year can save as much as $576 annually if they drive at 55 mph instead of 75 mph.

As for vehicles with other kinds of powertrains, the fuel efficiency of a diesel car drops from 55 mpg at 55 mph to 37 mpg at 75 mph. At the time of writing, diesel costs $6.35 per gallon in the U.S., meaning that the annual savings for 15,000 highway miles are over $800 per you if you stick to 55 mph instead of 75 mph.

Electrified models are not immune to the issue as they are also greatly affected by drag. According to the same study, a hybrid midsize sedan drops from 46 mpg at 55 mph to 33 mpg at 75 mph. Notably, hybrids reach their efficiency peak at 45 mph, where they return up to 55 mpg, meaning fast highway cruising negates much of the hybrid powertrain advantage . Bear in mind that these estimates are for sedans, meaning that boxier trucks and SUVs with a larger frontal area will have a greater penalty at higher speeds.

Finally, while we don't have access to equivalent data for EVs, range drops when you go faster, forcing you to spend more time charging. Still, EVs typically have favorable drag coefficient by design, and electricity costs are lower than gasoline and diesel. To conclude, drivers who are patient enough not to exceed 55 mph on the highway are going to have some spare cash at the end of the year. If you want you lower your fuel spending even further, be sure not to carry unnecessary weight or equipment that might increase drag .

article_paragraphs: You've probably sat around a campfire at some point in your life and figured out firsthand that plastic and heat don't mix. Whether you threw an empty soda bottle or marshmallow bag in and watched it shrivel up, or propped your sandals up on the stones around the fire and witnessed your soles melting, you get it.

Plastic is a pretty good insulator, but it has a pretty low melting point. ABS has a melting point of around 440 degrees Fahrenheit, while most available PLAs melt at 340-ish degrees. If you've spent any time looking at your engine's oil or coolant temperature gauges, you'll know that a running engine is pretty stable in the low 200-degree range, but the combustion chamber can get up to 2,500 degrees during the peak of the power stroke. Plastic doesn't stand a chance, which is why most engines are crafted from cast iron or aluminum.

We've already seen what happens when you try to use a 3D-printed cylinder head ; the results aren't pretty. With the kind of heat an engine sees, plastic just isn't the preferred material to work with. There are certainly some engines that have made extensive use of plastic, including the Torlon-based engines from Polimotor Research in the 1970s and 80s , but there isn't a high-enough-heat plastic to manage combustion chamber heat spikes, so a blend of metal and plastic is necessary.

YouTuber and mad scientist Alexander's Laboratory recently built and ran a pair of 3D-printed plastic engines, a single-cylinder and a parallel twin. We'll talk through both engines and their unique challenges in a second. First, we should take a step back and think about the implications of potentially building real working 3D-printed engines as prices come down and the technology both improves and becomes commonplace.

Have you ever built (or rebuilt) an engine for one of your project cars? There are just so many pieces and parts you have to buy, and there's so much measuring and clearance-checking to be done before the parts can all get bolted together. It's time-consuming and expensive, but the longest time you'll spend working on it is the shipping time to get all of the parts. Imagine if, someday, every engine in every car shared interchangeable components that could be stocked at any local auto parts store, and the rest could be 3D-printed at home. Wouldn't that be cool?

There are certainly still components that would need to be made out of metal, of course. The obvious first step would be to use metal for the combustion chamber, cylinder head, pistons, and crankshaft. You would also need to figure out a bearing system that works for the crankshaft and camshafts. Then there are things like the valves, valve springs, hardware, water pump components, and the accessory drive pullies.

Alexander is able to make most of his engines out of plastic, including the water pump and drive gears, but I'd go with metal for those on a full-scale engine, purely for longevity's sake. In the end, if you could make it work, you would have an engine significantly lighter than a comparable aluminum cylinder head and engine block unit. Recent research indicates swapping from a metal component to a 3D-printed plastic replacement cuts weight by 30% and costs by 15%. With enough research, you could add structural lattice inside some areas of components to make it even lighter, or allow better coolant flow to critical heat spots. Now this is exciting!

If you wanted to build a 3D-printed plastic engine, what steps would you need to take so it would run for more than a few seconds? As mentioned above, some metal is needed to keep it alive. Alexander strategically used machined steel for both the cylinder walls and the combustion chamber surface. This is smart, as it allows a sealing surface for the metal valves and the ability to thread in a common spark plug. The crankshaft is also metal, as is the surface of the pistons, but pretty much everything else comes straight off the printer.

raw_summary: In the early morning hours of August 22, 2003, in West Covina, California, vandals damaged one building and 125 SUVs across four dealerships and a private neighborhood with paint nd destroyed others with firebombs. article_paragraphs: In the early morning hours of August 22, 2003, in West Covina, California, vandals damaged one building and 125 SUVs across four dealerships and a private neighborhood with paint nd destroyed others with firebombs. The vandals spray-painted messages like "I love POLLUTION" and "SUV = TERRORISM". Most of all, they repeatedly painted the acronym "ELF," linking them to the Earth Liberation Front, a leaderless, loosely organized activist group. ELF targeted property and managed to avoid causing serious physical harm to anyone in hundreds of credited attacks from the late 1990s through the 2000s. The government branded ELF a terrorist group, partly because ELF used destructive tactics like arson, which is a common tool of militant groups . And, in fact, multiple SUVs were set on fire that night in 2003.

Either way, the government knew they were looking for passionate environmentalists. Within just a couple of weeks, the feds arrested a suspect, Josh Connole. Connole was a peace activist, vegetarian, and solar panel sales rep. He drove an EV and lived at a commune. All of those things seemed to make him a perfect fit for a particular kind of profile.

But Connole wasn't the guy. After his arrest was announced, a reporter at the LA Times received the first of multiple emails from "Tony Marsden" that read, "The police have the wrong man here. I was amongst those responsible for the SUV attacks."

Was the sender concerned about an innocent man paying for their crimes? Maybe, but some gloating was involved, too. "We left plenty of clues, none of them pointing to Josh," the message said, then added smugly, "The FBI hasn't seemed to pick up on any of them, which makes the whole ordeal very boring for us, the true culprits." To prove his involvement, he noted that he had spray-painted an equation by Leonhard Euler, an 18th-century Swiss mathematician, on one of the SUVs. That was a detail that hadn't been released to the public.

His boredom wouldn't last long, as the emails would be traced to his college, Caltech. Apparently, he couldn't be bothered to send the emails from another location. Law enforcement seized multiple computers from the school and found a cache of the email messages on one of the machines, sent right after the sender checked his own messages. The actual sender of the email, as you might have guessed, was not named "Tony Marsden." His name was William "Billy" Cottrell, and he was going for his PhD in theoretical physics at Caltech.

If Billy thought that he could successfully deny sending the emails or his involvement in the spree, that wouldn't last long. Investigators soon matched his DNA to a headband found at the scene of the crime. For Billy, the jig was up.

At first, Billy told investigators he wouldn't implicate anyone else in the spree, but later blamed the arson part of it entirely on his friends, Tyler Johnson and Michie Oe. According to Billy, whose statements are a little self-serving and should probably be taken with a grain of salt, Tyler and Michie showed up that night and convinced him to go spray-paint some SUVs with them. Billy wouldn't have seen this as an odd request, since he and Tyler had recently planned to plaster a couple of hundred SUVs with bumper stickers that said, "My SUV supports terrorism," though that plan fell through.

The three hit one dealership, then another before moving on to a private neighborhood where they vandalized some more SUVs. It was in that neighborhood where Tyler, according to Billy, set the first SUV on fire. Billy claimed that Tyler had never told him about plans to set anything on fire, and he objected when Tyler used the first firebomb. Supposedly, Tyler said it wouldn't happen again. But Tyler didn't stop, and more SUVs were set ablaze at the last dealership hit that night. In fact, a Molotov cocktail accidentally hit Billy's clothes, setting them on fire. He quickly took off his shirt, which is how his headband wound up on the ground for investigators to find.

Almost seven years ago, while clutching a laptop, my phone, and a notebook in a sea of Tesla fans, I watched head designer Franz von Holzhausen throw a metal, baseball-sized ball at the driver’s-side window of the Cybertruck . The result was cracked glass — actually, two by the end of the presentation — and some awkward jokes and chuckling by CEO Elon Musk .

I have witnessed a number of stunning, odd, and fantastical moments at Tesla events. But the Cybertruck reveal was the most interesting — and not because of the postapocalyptic design. It was the crowd.

When the truck rolled out onto the stage, I watched attendees gasp, some in revulsion. There was mumbling (“This certainly can’t be the Cybertruck ?” I heard Tesla superfans whisper). And yes, there were cheers. The momentary shock of Musk’s biggest fans was quickly replaced by support, acceptance, and finally, endorsement.
It moved like a wave over the crowd. By the time attendees were waiting in line for Cybertruck rides, the mood had shifted. Everyone was a fan.

That fandom carried over to Cybertruck reservations, which skyrocketed to 1 million, Musk said during a third-quarter earnings call in 2023. But it never made the leap to actual sales. Industry experts estimate about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023.
And now the Cybertruck is headed to the scrap pile. Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, Musk said Friday.

Was the vehicle too edgy? Maybe, but this was always going to be a niche market. I believe more practical reasons dampened sales. Musk promised the Cybertruck would have a 500-mile range and a price tag under $40,000. It achieved neither, senior reporter Sean O’Kane noted in his report .

The injured Jorge Martin laboured to seventh, meanwhile, and is now 60 points back from Marquez, with 74 available.

Bezzecchi had kept the lead from pole at the start, with an Aprilia 1-2 established as Raul Fernandez worked his way past Marquez - shortly after having lunged past Trackhouse team-mate Ai Ogura at Turn 1.
Marquez paced himself quite gingerly through the opening phase of the race, allowing the Aprilias to break away and even ceding third place to Pedro Acosta on the third lap.
But Acosta, seemingly in trouble with front tyre pressures and desperately trying to get temperature into the rubber, rolled out to let Marquez back through a few laps later.
Marquez then shook off his KTM pursuer as the race ticked over into its second half, then came up on and overtook Fernandez - who is still managing an index finger injury - for second.

Fernandez held on to third place despite the threat of team-mate Ogura from behind, Ogura the second of three riders who Acosta waved through while trying to keep his tyre pressures in the right window.

raw_title: Even California’s Biggest Ports Aren’t Betting On Hydrogen For Ships
title: Even California's Biggest Ports Aren't Betting On Hydrogen For Ships
raw_summary: California has been one of hydrogen’s most enthusiastic supporters for two decades. The state has subsidized hydrogen vehicles, backed refueling networks, supported fuel-cell buses and trucks, invested in hydrogen production and kept the technology prominent in its zero-emission transportation policies. Los Angeles and Long Beach, the two enormous ports that anchor America’s Pacific container trade, have been part of that enthusiasm. So when these ports produce a comprehensive assessment of future marine fuels and leave hydrogen out of their detailed deep-sea shipping plans, it deserves attention well beyond California. The Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , released in October, is the product of a substantial examination of shipping fleets, carrier preferences, fuel availability and infrastructure costs. The ports recommend developing commercial methanol bunkering demonstrations, continuing existing ship-to-ship LNG bunkering arrangements and avoiding major new fuel terminals until demand becomes credible. Hydrogen, the molecule that California has spent so much money promoting for transportation, did not make the cut for detailed quantitative deep-sea fuel planning.

article_paragraphs: California has been one of hydrogen’s most enthusiastic supporters for two decades. The state has subsidized hydrogen vehicles, backed refueling networks, supported fuel-cell buses and trucks, invested in hydrogen production and kept the technology prominent in its zero-emission transportation policies. Los Angeles and Long Beach, the two enormous ports that anchor America’s Pacific container trade, have been part of that enthusiasm. So when these ports produce a comprehensive assessment of future marine fuels and leave hydrogen out of their detailed deep-sea shipping plans, it deserves attention well beyond California.

The Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , released in October, is the product of a substantial examination of shipping fleets, carrier preferences, fuel availability and infrastructure costs. The ports recommend developing commercial methanol bunkering demonstrations, continuing existing ship-to-ship LNG bunkering arrangements and avoiding major new fuel terminals until demand becomes credible. Hydrogen, the molecule that California has spent so much money promoting for transportation, did not make the cut for detailed quantitative deep-sea fuel planning.

This isn’t a state government announcing the end of hydrogen subsidies. It is arguably more revealing. Two commercially important institutions have examined what the ships serving them are likely to use, considered the infrastructure they would have to provide and declined to spend the next decade preparing a major hydrogen bunkering business.

California’s hydrogen story has repeatedly confused technical possibility with commercial demand. Fuel-cell passenger cars proved they could operate, but struggled with expensive fuel, unreliable stations and battery-electric competition. Hydrogen buses and trucks have faced many of the same issues, often compounded by the economics of supplying fuel to fleets. Ports have supported hydrogen demonstrations because eliminating diesel exhaust matters enormously to nearby communities, but a successful demonstration does not establish that the resulting system is the best commercial solution.

Deep-sea shipping adds a particularly difficult set of constraints. A container vessel requires immense amounts of energy over long voyages. Hydrogen’s low volumetric energy density, expensive handling and demanding onboard storage make the fuel system difficult to accommodate economically. The problem extends beyond the ship to production, transportation, storage and bunkering equipment. There is little reason for a port authority to build a hydrogen fuel network when shipping lines are not ordering a commercially significant fleet that would use it.

The ports’ survey reinforces the commercial judgment. Of 38 shipping lines contacted, 19 responded. Nine expressed varying degrees of interest or commitment concerning methanol, but only one did so for hydrogen. That is a survey of carrier intentions, rather than binding fuel contracts, and the researchers examined other evidence as well. Still, it is difficult to turn one interested carrier into a compelling investment case for expensive hydrogen infrastructure.

The contrast with methanol is instructive. Methanol is a liquid under ordinary conditions and fits into a mature global chemical-handling industry. Existing storage and bunkering equipment can be adapted instead of requiring an entirely new cryogenic or high-pressure fuel network. Long Beach is already offering a $1 million incentive for an initial commercial-scale methanol bunkering operation, an approach that can test operational feasibility without committing to an enormous permanent facility.

I have a personal interest in that choice because I had to correct my own shipping-fuel forecast. Last year, I published Mea Culpa: Biomethanol Will Be A Major Shipping Fuel . I had previously given too much weight to vegetable-oil-derived fuels for shipping and insufficient weight to aviation’s competition for those feedstocks. I had also underestimated how far cheaper batteries could displace marine fuel demand. My revised assessment favours electricity for inland and short-sea shipping, with sustainable biomethanol becoming a primary liquid fuel for the remaining deep-sea requirement. The ports’ decision is consistent with preparing infrastructure for that possibility, although it does not establish that their future fuel supplies will be renewable.

raw_title: These 5 Italian Exotics Are More Dependable Than The Finicky Supercars Of Yesteryear
title: These 5 Italian Exotics Are More Dependable Than The Finicky Supercars Of Yesteryear
raw_summary: Supercar ownership has been, and likely always will be, quite a scary proposition for newcomers, save for those who have pockets deep enough to not even care how much the next service or repair bill will cost. However, modern engineering and the cross-platform hardware that exists in many a modern supercar makes ownership a little more approachable compared to the exotics that came before them. For example, classic Ferraris like the F355 and Testarossa require engine-out servicing on an uncomfortably frequent basis, while electrical gremlins, rattling cam chains, and inadequate braking systems trouble the pre-Audi-era Lamborghinis. Now, look at their modern counterparts. The Ferrari 458 Italia is chain-driven and capable of six-figure mileages, plus its modern DCT transmission is impressively durable and free of pricey clutch changes. Meanwhile, modern Lamborghinis share a lot of hardware with mass-market models from within the Volkswagen-Audi group as well as some other mainstream automakers, which, for buyers that know where to look, brings down servicing and maintenance costs dramatically.

For example, classic Ferraris like the F355 and Testarossa require engine-out servicing on an uncomfortably frequent basis, while electrical gremlins, rattling cam chains, and inadequate braking systems trouble the pre-Audi-era Lamborghinis.

Now, look at their modern counterparts. The Ferrari 458 Italia is chain-driven and capable of six-figure mileages, plus its modern DCT transmission is impressively durable and free of pricey clutch changes. Meanwhile, modern Lamborghinis share a lot of hardware with mass-market models from within the Volkswagen-Audi group as well as some other mainstream automakers, which, for buyers that know where to look, brings down servicing and maintenance costs dramatically.

To prove our point, this piece covers seven modern Italian supercars that offer a surprisingly worry-free ownership experience — from the aforementioned models through to more entry-level supercars like the Ferrari California. The supercars on this list all utilize proven powerplants that have all been on the market for at least a decade, are typically simple and robust in design, and are backed up by numerous examples with six-figure mileages still on the roads today. As a result, the Italian supercars on this list all have no known major mechanical issues, straightforward servicing and global warranty coverage, and a reputation for reliability among enthusiasts. And above all else, they are way more dependable than many pre-2000 models that preceded them.

A high-performance, limited-run Alfa Romeo and dependable, all in the same sentence? That's right. Including the 8C wasn't some sort of mistake, and this Alfa's case is actually quite easy to argue. First off, the 8C isn't totally void of faults. Alfa Romeo issued a recall in 2009 that affected the front and rear lower ball joints, and at least one 8C randomly combusted as a result of a suspected electrical gremlin. However, even $70 million 250 GTOs catch fire from time to time, so perhaps that's just part and parcel of Italian supercar ownership.

That aside, the 8C is largely based on a Maserati GranTurismo, rather than being some custom creation featuring heaps of unique parts. It's also motivated by the same Ferrari-Maserati F136 — a notoriously well-built V8 that also featured in the Ferrari F430 and 458. What this means for owners is that finding a specialist familiar with this engine shouldn't be a problem. Though the F136 is considered relatively dependable as long as basic maintenance is kept on top of.

Some of the factors that make the F136 more robust than older Ferrari V8s are chain-driven cams, a completely new, stiff aluminum block, forged pistons and a hardened-steel crankshaft. Owners also appreciate the fact that there's no engine-out servicing. We even mentioned it among the greatest engines of the last decade .

Given the super exclusive nature of these cars, most 8Cs seem to be kept as cherished weekend toys and don't see heaps of use, but the proven underpinnings mean that, given the chance, they could probably cover significant mileage without major hiccups. Compare the F136 V8 to the complex and low-production engines fitted to previous special Alfas like the '70s Montreal, and the 8C looks like quite a tempting prospect.

For all the same reasons why the 8C is great, the California is just as good. It's another grand tourer supercar that uses the F136. In this guise, the V8 produces 460 hp and 358 lb-ft of torque from a 4.3-liter displacement. One of the real benefits to the California is that it was sold with the "Ferrari Genuine Maintenance" program packaged in — alongside other contemporary Ferrari models. That provided owners with seven years' worth of free servicing, and it wasn't capped at one service per year.

raw_title: What Do The Red And Yellow Dots On Tires Mean?
title: What Do The Red And Yellow Dots On Tires Mean?
raw_summary: New tires can come with some genuine surprises outside of a potentially wild bill. Sometimes that comes in the form of grip. Other times it comes in the form of smoothness on the road. In addition, most come with a couple of small painted dots that almost nobody ever explains. While things like the colored stripes on the tire don't really matter after their initial sale, these dots are key for anyone installing the tire down the road. Here's a quick breakdown of what each dot is and what it signifies. To be short and sweet, there are typically two dots on a modern tire. First, you'll find a yellow dot. It signifies the lightest part of the tire in question when tested by the manufacturer. Second, a red dot alerts a tire balancer to the point of maximum force variation. Both of those deserve a little unpacking and explanation.
summary: New tires can come with some genuine surprises outside of a potentially wild bill. Sometimes that comes in the form of grip. Other times it comes in the form of smoothness on the road. In addition, most come with a couple of small painted dots that almost nobody ever explains.
article_paragraphs: New tires can come with some genuine surprises outside of a potentially wild bill. Sometimes that comes in the form of grip. Other times it comes in the form of smoothness on the road. In addition, most come with a couple of small painted dots that almost nobody ever explains. While things like the colored stripes on the tire don't really matter after their initial sale, these dots are key for anyone installing the tire down the road. Here's a quick breakdown of what each dot is and what it signifies.

To be short and sweet, there are typically two dots on a modern tire. First, you'll find a yellow dot. It signifies the lightest part of the tire in question when tested by the manufacturer. Second, a red dot alerts a tire balancer to the point of maximum force variation. Both of those deserve a little unpacking and explanation.

Of the two dots, the yellow one is easier for most of us to understand. Despite looking like a perfectly symmetrical product, tires almost always have some variation in density from one point of their circumference to another, even the latest and greatest tires from Michelin with AI tech . Marking the lightest point around the tire gives the installer a reference for where to seat the tire on the wheel.

Why does that matter if a wheel is perfectly balanced all the way around? Well, it wouldn't in that case, but the valve stem is generally the wheel's heaviest point. Aligning the tire's yellow dot with that location brings the lighter part of one component together with the heavier part of the other. For a tire balancer, that means fewer tests, hopefully fewer weights, and a quicker turnaround time. That benefits everybody from the tire shop to the technician to the vehicle owner.

Now, let's dig into the more difficult dot to understand. The red dot addresses how the tire behaves when it's under load. As a loaded tire rotates, it generates what's called radial force variation. The red mark identifies the peak of that variation. Calling it the tire's "high point" is common shorthand, but there's more involved than its unloaded shape. Ultimately, that point can create vibrations if it's not accounted for.

Installers can check a wheel for its point of minimum radial runout, which is typically marked with a notch or colored mark. Interestingly, at least in my experience as the manager of a wheel and tire shop, the red mark matters more than the yellow one. A misaligned red dot can cause more vibration and discomfort in the cabin than a misaligned yellow dot. Of course, even an AI-driven robotic tire changer is going to add appropriate wheel weights as needed, regardless of where the red and yellow dots fall.

Sometimes that comes in the form of grip.
Other times it comes in the form of smoothness on the road.

raw_title: If You Could Only Drive Cars From One Brand For The Rest Of Your Life, Which Automaker Are You Choosing?
title: If You Could Only Drive Cars From One Brand For The Rest Of Your Life, Which Automaker Are You Choosing?
raw_summary: Some of you lot have told Jalopnik that branding doesn't matter , but let's face it, branding really does matter, because loyalty matters . From the salt you put on your eggs in the morning to the car you drive every day, your purchase tells that brand it's doing something right. It's why some movie franchises have more than 10 sequels even if the last 9 films were terrible. It's why companies constantly find themselves sleeping with data giants. This weekend's question was inspired by a trend I saw popping up on social media over the last few days, where individuals are asked if they had to watch movies for 24 hours, and all of the films had to feature the work of one actor, who would they pick? I would choose John Malkovich, who has been in a ton of brilliant movies across the spectrum that would certainly keep any decent cinephile entertained. He's just a great actor. How can you argue with that?

This weekend's question was inspired by a trend I saw popping up on social media over the last few days, where individuals are asked if they had to watch movies for 24 hours, and all of the films had to feature the work of one actor, who would they pick? I would choose John Malkovich, who has been in a ton of brilliant movies across the spectrum that would certainly keep any decent cinephile entertained. He's just a great actor. How can you argue with that?

Getting to today's question, though, I've modified it a bit for our purposes. Assuming the brand is still in existence for that long, if you could only drive cars from one automaker for the rest of your life, which brand are you choosing?

One company initially came to my mind for this week's question, and it's in the running for what will replace my Mercedes CLS when its time comes. I reckon I still have a few more years until I have to worry about that, but I would willingly pledge my life's driving experiences to Subaru. The vehicles Subaru offers have long been on my list as hopefuls to own, doubling as decently fun on both the road and in the dirt, which has long been an attractive attribute to me. This is where my Mercedes tends to fail, even if I did once use it to go on an outdoor dirt biking adventure in the mountains. It managed, but a Subaru would have been much better.

It helps that Subaru has, for the longest time, continually sold a sedan with a manual transmission, with the current offering being the WRX . Sure, its lineup is mostly crossovers, but the Japanese brand has stayed true to its heritage, something many automakers constantly fumble. Subaru also makes vehicles that are near-indestructible. I've encountered many in the wild with well over 300,000 miles, beaten and bruised but still running. For bonus points, it certainly doesn't hurt that Subaru does the whole doggy adoption display at basically every auto show in the nation.

Here's where you readers come in. It's time to buck up and pick a brand to drive you into the sunset that is the end of life. I thought about asking you to keep it to brands that exist now, but if you have strong feelings about a past manufacturer, so be it. I'm curious how you would keep defunct cars running for the next handful of decades, but as crafty folks that continue to endure the hobby, you find a way. You always find a way.
